title: SI units & prefixes
examples: What is the base unit for length?
How do I use prefixes like kilo and milli?
Can you give an example of a derived unit?

explain.say: Today we are learning about units of measurement. These units help us measure things in science. We use a system called SI units for this.
Some units are basic measurements called base units. These are the fundamental measurements in science. For example, the base unit for length is the metre.
Other units combine base units to measure things. These are called derived units. Speed is a good example of a derived unit. Speed is metres per second.
We also use prefixes to make units bigger or smaller. Kilo means one thousand. Milli means one thousandth. For example, four hundred fifty milliampere is zero point four five ampere.

faq.q: What is the difference between base and derived units?
faq.a: Base units are fundamental measurements like length or time. Derived units combine these base units, such as volume which is length times length times length.
asks: How do I know if a unit is derived?

faq.q: What is the base unit for mass?
faq.a: The base unit for mass is the kilogram. This is one of the seven fundamental units in the SI system.
asks: What unit do we use for weight?
Is the gram a base unit?

faq.a: The prefix kilo means one thousand. It multiplies the base unit by one thousand. For example, one kilometre is one thousand metres.
asks: What is the meaning of 'k' in science?
If I see 'k' I should multiply by what?

faq.q: What is the base unit for electric current?
faq.a: The base unit for electric current is the ampere. This unit measures the flow of electrical charge.
asks: Is the volt related to the base unit?

faq.q: How do I convert between prefixes?
faq.a: You need to know the relationship between the prefixes. For example, one metre is one thousand millimetres. You are essentially multiplying or dividing by powers of ten.
asks: Do I always multiply when going from milli to base?
What is the rule for changing prefixes?

facts: The SI system uses seven base units for fundamental measurements.
Length is measured in metres, and time is measured in seconds.
Derived units are formed by combining base units, like speed in metres per second.
The prefix 'milli' represents one one-thousandth of the base unit.

quiz.say: What is the SI base unit for electric current?
quiz.why: The ampere is the specific base unit used to measure electric current in the SI system.

wrong.1: The volt is actually a derived unit used for potential difference, not the base unit for current.
wrong.2: The ohm is a unit used to measure electrical resistance, which is a derived quantity.
wrong.3: The watt measures power, which is a derived unit involving energy and time.

quiz.why: Since kilo means one thousand, you multiply three point five by one thousand to get three thousand five hundred metres.

wrong.0: This mistake happens if you divide by one hundred instead of multiplying by one thousand.
wrong.1: While scientific notation is correct, the question asks for the full number value in metres.
wrong.2: This suggests multiplying by one hundred, which is incorrect for converting kilometres to metres.

quiz.say: What is the unit for force?
quiz.why: Force is a derived unit calculated as mass times acceleration, giving us the newton.

wrong.1: Although this is the correct dimensional formula, the newton is the accepted standard unit name.
wrong.2: This combination is incorrect because it misses the required factor of acceleration, which is another metre per second squared.
wrong.3: This unit is incorrect because it does not account for the time element in acceleration.
